newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia opposition head says Milosevic under threat.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition head says Milosevic under threat.

text.p: The leader of Serbia's opposition coalition, which claims it is being unlawfully denied an election victory, on Friday said its protests threatened the long rule of President Slobodan Milosevic.

Demonstrators jammed the centre of some of Serbia's biggest towns on Friday, at the end of a week of protests against attempts by Milosevic's ruling Socialists to annull opposition victories in last Sunday's local elections.
Zoran Djindjic, 44, who leads the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition said the protests showed how little real support there is for Milosevic, in power since 1987.
"It puts in question the basic principles of his authority," Djindjic told Reuters in an interview.
"He's not losing much in terms of real power but psychologically he's losing a lot because it's clear now that he's not the only authority."
The charismatic young leader, expected to become the next mayor of Belgrade, underlined his point in a speech to some 10,000 supporters who gathered outside his party headquarters.

"They (the Socialist Party) are still living in the 15th century if they don't know that we won. Let them look in the streets and realise the opposition won," he told the crowd braving persistent rain.
Djindjic heads the Democratic Party (DS), one of three parties allied in the Zajedno coalition.
Analysts say the opposition victory has taken the Socialists by total surprise, prompting them to resort to annullments.
This has provoked an outcry both at home and abroad and alienated some members of the leftist coalition which scored a resounding victory at federal elections almost three weeks ago.
The Nova Democratija party, close to Milosevic, on Thursday denounced election rigging and called for the people's will to be respected. Its headquarters were petrol bombed hours later.

While Djindjic said the massive and unprecedented show of public support was encouraging, he said international support could make the difference between success and failure in their campaign to have the election results recognised.
"What would help would be to employ the already proved method in which (U.S. President Bill) Clinton or (French President Jacques) Chirac would telephone Milosevic," he said.
Foreign pressure has swayed Milosevic in the past.
He conceded the Zajedno leaders were debating their options if the authorities failed to confirm the election results by Sunday evening when a legal deadline for declaring them expires.
"That's going to be the most difficult political decision. One option is to call on the people to mount the final demonstration, the biggest yet," he said.

The other option was to participate in a third round of voting "which is very risky because we don't have any guarantees that they won't try to falsify the results like they did the last time," he said.
